verdict.summary: Any signed-in GitHub user can register an OAuth app, and any GitHub user can authorize it right away. The docs reviewed show no provider review for this. The real limits are organization owners, who must approve the app before it can reach org data, and GitHub Marketplace review, which only applies if you want a listing.
verdict.approval_wait: None for registration or public use. Organizations that restrict OAuth apps need an owner to approve your app. Marketplace listing review is optional and its timeline is not documented.

gates.name: Registered OAuth app (owner's own account)
gates.unlocks: You can authorize your own GitHub account through your app via Composio.
limits: Requires a signed-in GitHub account; the app is owned by a personal account or an organization where you are an admin
Max 100 OAuth apps per user or organization
Up to 10 callback URLs per app
'Expire user access tokens' is on by default: access tokens last 8 hours, refresh tokens last 6 months without use

gates.name: Other GitHub users and organization members
gates.unlocks: Teammates or invited users can authorize the app. For organizations with OAuth app access restrictions, an owner's approval also lets the app reach org resources.
limits: GitHub has no test-user allowlist. Any GitHub user who opens the authorize URL can grant access.
New organizations restrict OAuth apps by default, so members must request approval from an owner
Org owners can turn off app access requests entirely
Users can edit requested scopes on the consent screen, so you may get less than you asked for
Signing in the same user 10 times in one hour forces re-authorization
gates.time_to_reach: Immediate for personal-account data. For restricted orgs it depends on when an owner approves.

gates.name: Public use (optional GitHub Marketplace listing)
gates.unlocks: Any GitHub user can authorize the app. A Marketplace listing adds discoverability and paid plans.
limits: 2,000 access token requests per hour per OAuth app; going over can temporarily block new token generation
API calls use each user's limit of 5,000 requests per hour
Device flow: 50 user-code submissions per hour per app
Marketplace listing: privacy policy, publisher contact info, description, pricing plan, support link, and the app must integrate beyond authentication
Paid Marketplace plans: the app must belong to a verified-publisher organization and should have at least 200 users
gates.time_to_reach: Public use needs no extra time. A Marketplace listing takes as long as the listing review does (timeline not documented).

steps.title: Choose between an OAuth app and a GitHub App
steps.detail: GitHub says GitHub Apps are generally preferred because they use fine-grained, per-repository permissions and short-lived tokens. An authorized OAuth app can reach everything the user can access. Pick an OAuth app if you need Composio's standard GitHub OAuth2 config or enterprise-level resources.
gotchas: OAuth apps can't use granular permissions. Scopes are coarse, and repo gives full read/write access to private repos.

steps.title: Sign in and decide which account owns the app
steps.detail: Sign in to GitHub. Register the app under your personal account, or under an organization where you are an admin. If you might sell the app on Marketplace later, register it under an organization from the start.
gotchas: To sell an app on Marketplace, a personal-account app must first be transferred to an organization.

steps.title: Get the exact callback URL from Composio
steps.detail: In Composio, create a GitHub auth config that uses your own OAuth app, and copy the callback URL it shows. The research found two candidate URLs, so use the one in your auth config, not one from memory.

values.label: Redirect URI
values.value: Composio callback URL (see the Composio callout on this page)

gotchas: The research found two candidate URLs: https://backend.composio.dev/api/v1/auth-apps/add (toolkit listing) and https://backend.composio.dev/api/v3/toolkits/auth/callback (authorize probe). The token exchange checks redirect_uri, so a mismatch makes it fail.

steps.title: Open the New OAuth App form
steps.detail: Go to your profile Settings, then Developer settings, then click OAuth apps in the left sidebar and click New OAuth App. For an organization-owned app, start from the organization's settings instead.

steps.title: Fill in and register the application
steps.detail: Enter the Application name and Homepage URL, plus an optional description, and paste the Composio callback into Authorization callback URL. Leave Enable Device Flow unchecked unless you need headless/CLI sign-in. Then click Register application.

values.label: Redirect URI
values.value: Composio callback URL (see the Composio callout on this page)

gotchas: You can add up to 10 callback URLs, for example separate dev and prod callbacks.
The implicit grant is not supported. Use the authorization code (web application) flow.

steps.title: Decide on 'Expire user access tokens'
steps.detail: This checkbox is on by default for new apps. With it on, access tokens expire after 8 hours and refresh tokens after 6 months without use. Each refresh returns a new refresh token, which must be stored. Leave it on only if your Composio setup handles refresh. Otherwise turn it off.
gotchas: Turning expiry on later does not expire existing tokens. Users must sign in again to get expiring tokens.
Non-expiring tokens are still revoked automatically after one year without use.

steps.title: Copy the client ID and client secret into Composio
steps.detail: On the registered app's settings page, copy the Client ID and create a client secret. Paste both into your Composio GitHub auth config. Keep the secret in a secret store, not in source code.
gotchas: The research did not document the exact client-secret button label. Look for it on the app's settings page.

steps.title: Pick the smallest scope set you need
steps.detail: Composio's default list (repo, user, gist, notifications, project, workflow, codespace) is broad. Remove scopes your agent doesn't use. Use narrower ones where they work, such as public_repo, repo:status, write:repo_hook or read:user. Scopes are space-delimited in the scope parameter.
gotchas: Users can edit the requested scopes on the consent screen, so check which scopes were actually granted.

steps.title: Run a test authorization with your own account
steps.detail: Start a connection from Composio, approve it on GitHub's consent screen, and check that the token exchange succeeds and an API call works. The authorization code expires after 10 minutes, and the redirect_uri must match the registered callback.
gotchas: PKCE supports S256 only. The plain method is rejected.
Send an unguessable state value to guard against forged requests.

steps.title: Get organization approval for org resources
steps.detail: If your users' organizations restrict OAuth apps (the default for new orgs), each member must request approval and an org owner must approve your app. Until that happens, the app can't reach that org's repos. Tell users about this step when they onboard.
gotchas: Owners can turn off app access requests completely. Then the owner has to approve your app directly.
The exemption for privileged OAuth apps covers only apps GitHub owns. It does not cover yours.

steps.title: Plan for rate limits before wider rollout
steps.detail: Keep token requests under 2,000 per hour per app, and avoid signing in the same user repeatedly (10 sign-ins in an hour forces re-authorization). API calls count against each user's 5,000 requests per hour. Rate-limit increases are granted per OAuth app.

steps.title: (Optional) Submit a GitHub Marketplace listing
steps.detail: You need this only if you want the app listed or sold on GitHub Marketplace. Public use doesn't require it. Requirements: a privacy policy link, publisher contact info, a description, a pricing plan, a working support link, and integration beyond authentication. Paid plans also need a verified-publisher organization and about 200 or more users.
gotchas: Paid apps must handle Marketplace purchase events.

requirements.item: Signed-in GitHub account (personal, or admin of the owning organization)
requirements.detail: The developer settings page requires sign-in. Apps can be owned by a personal account or an organization where you are an admin.

requirements.item: Homepage URL and authorization callback URL
requirements.detail: Required fields on the registration form. You can register up to 10 callback URLs.
Needed for each organization that restricts OAuth app access. Restrictions are on by default for new organizations.

requirements.item: Privacy policy, support contact, pricing plan (Marketplace only)
requirements.detail: Needed only for a Marketplace listing. The app must be publicly available and do more than authentication.

requirements.item: Verified-publisher organization and about 200 users (paid Marketplace plans only)
requirements.detail: Paid plans need a verified-publisher organization that owns the app, and OAuth apps should have at least 200 users.

scopes.effect: Full read/write access to public and private repos, plus org projects, invitations, team memberships and webhooks. GitHub has no review tier for it, but org owners and users will look closely at it. Use public_repo or repo:status if they cover your needs.
Read/write access to the profile. Includes user:email and user:follow. Use read:user if you only need to read the profile.
Part of Composio's default list. Remove any your agent doesn't use, since users see every requested scope and can edit them.
Requests an expiring token plus a refresh token for one sign-in, even if the app-level expiry setting is off.

blockers.symptom: Users can authorize the app, but org repositories are missing or access is denied for an organization.
blockers.cause: The organization has OAuth app access restrictions enabled (the default for new orgs), and an owner has not approved your app.
blockers.fix: Have the member request approval, and have an org owner approve the app in the organization's OAuth app settings.

blockers.cause: The redirect_uri doesn't match the registered callback (the Composio callback is ambiguous), or the code was used more than 10 minutes after it was issued.
blockers.fix: Register the exact callback shown in your Composio auth config, and exchange the code right away.

blockers.symptom: Connections stop working after about 8 hours.
blockers.cause: 'Expire user access tokens' is on by default, and the integration is not refreshing tokens.
blockers.fix: Turn the setting off, or make sure refresh is handled and that each new refresh token is stored.

blockers.symptom: New tokens can't be issued temporarily (outage).
blockers.cause: The app went over 2,000 access token requests per hour.
blockers.fix: Cut down repeated sign-ins and token requests. Reuse stored tokens.

composio.note: Start with Composio's managed GitHub OAuth app for prototyping. Register your own OAuth app when you want your own branding on the consent screen, your own client ID and secret, your own rate-limit budget (2,000 token requests per hour per app), or fewer scopes than the default list, which includes repo, workflow and codespace. Paste the callback URL from your Composio auth config exactly as shown.

evidence.claim: repo grants full read/write access to public and private repositories.

evidence.quote: OAuth apps can't use granular permissions.

evidence.quote: An *authorized* OAuth app has access to all of the user's or organization owner's accessible resources.

open_questions: The Composio callback URL to register is unclear: the toolkit listing gives /api/v1/auth-apps/add and the authorize probe used /api/v3/toolkits/auth/callback. Use the URL shown in your Composio auth config, and check with Composio if unsure.
It is not confirmed whether Composio's GitHub integration handles refresh for expiring (8-hour) tokens. This decides whether to leave 'Expire user access tokens' on.
No Marketplace listing review timeline was found.
No documented manual review for standard OAuth app registration was found. The 'no review' conclusion is inferred.
How GitHub rejects unknown client IDs was not confirmed: the probe redirected to sign-in.
It was not confirmed whether PKCE is required for every OAuth app token exchange.
The exact client-secret generation UI label was not captured in the findings.
